title: Nurturing the Whole Being: An Indian Perspective
summary: 'Personality' comes from the Latin 'persona', a mask worn by actors in Greek and Roman theatres; it means the external appearance accessible to others. Indian thinkers saw human existence as an integrated structure with spiritual and material aspects; in the Upanishads the Self (Atman, consciousness) is the real core of personality, eternal and immutable. Personality is not physical appearance only; it extends to physical, social and spiritual levels. The Bhagavad Gita emphasises the Tri-guna view and the Upanishads the Panch Kosha theory; Sri Aurobindo gave a comprehensive system based on consciousness.

All nature is a combination of three Gunas: Sattwa (light), Rajas (dynamism) and Tamas (lethargy or inertia). Development moves from Tamas to Rajas to Sattwa; the highest stage is beyond the three gunas. Sattwik person: moderate in eating, sleeping and activity, meditates regularly, works as worship, loves and helps people, radiates the light of knowledge (Guru Nanak, Kabir, Meera, Thyagaraj). Rajasik person: very active, dynamic, addicted to work, restless without work, likes spicy food and entertainment, found in the business world. Tamasik person: dislikes work, rises late, idle, dirty, lethargic; failures in life. Each person is a combination of the three in different degrees; personality development means the right proportion – Rajas is necessary to some extent, Tamas should be kept to a minimum.

Existence has five layers or sheaths from outer to inner: (1) Annamaya Kosha (food sheath) – the physical body formed from food; healthy development shown by fitness, agility, stamina and endurance, good motor skills and eye–hand coordination; (2) Pranamaya Kosha (vital sheath) – the five Pranas: Prana (perception), Apana (excretion), Samana (digestion), Vyana (circulation) and Udana (thinking, capacity for self-education); it regulates the food sheath; signs: enthusiasm, effective voice, suppleness, perseverance, leadership, discipline, honesty and nobility; (3) Manomaya Kosha (mental sheath) – feelings and emotions; the mind interprets sense impressions and stores memories; regulates the vital sheath; strengthened by prayer and resolutions; (4) Vijnanamaya Kosha (intellectual sheath) – imagination, memory, knowledge, insight; the intellect (buddhi) discriminates and judges, takes rational decisions and can penetrate the 'realms unknown' while mind travels only in the 'realms known'; (5) Anandamaya Kosha (blissful sheath) – the innermost, made of vasanas (desires) in the subconscious as in deep sleep; creativity, joy and bliss; it controls the intellectual sheath. Harmony of all koshas brings joy; the Atman is distinct from the five sheaths like the wearer from clothes.

Annamaya: regular eating habits, right food, exercise, games, jogging, walking and asanas. Pranamaya: pranayama and breathing exercises. Manomaya: study of good literature (poems, novels, essays). Vijnanamaya: intellect-challenging activities – debates, problem solving, study techniques, small research projects, evaluating books, interviewing eminent persons. Anandamaya: going beyond the tiny self, identifying with community, country and the world, extending consciousness in contemplation to the earth, sun, stars and universe, linking individual and universal consciousness.
## Sri Aurobindo on levels of consciousness

Two systems act together. The concentric system is a series of rings: the outer circle has awareness of the physical, vital (pranic) and mental sheaths; the inner circle is the inner mind in touch with universal mind or Supreme Energy; the innermost core is the Psychic being, a spark of the Divine, also called Atman. The vertical system is a staircase of planes of consciousness from the lowest, the inconscient, to the highest, Sat-Chit-Ananda; humans have climbed from unicellular life and our evolution is not complete.

It extends to physical, social and spiritual levels, with the Atman as its core.

The physical body, the outermost food sheath formed from food and returning to food.

sa: Explain the Indian concept of personality.
Personality is the whole of existence – physical, social and spiritual – with the Atman as its core, not merely external appearance.
Describe the three gunas and the three types of persons.
Sattwa is light (meditative, loving), Rajas is dynamism (active, restless) and Tamas is inertia (idle, lethargic). Everyone has all three; development keeps Tamas minimum.

The vital sheath comprising the five Pranas for perception, excretion, digestion, circulation and thinking; it regulates the body, and its healthy development shows in enthusiasm, discipline and honesty.
Manomaya is the mental sheath of feelings, emotions and memories; Vijnanamaya is the intellectual sheath of imagination, knowledge, insight and discriminating decisions.
How can the Annamaya and Pranamaya Koshas be developed?
Annamaya by regular, right food, exercise, games and asanas; Pranamaya by pranayama and breathing exercises.
A series of rings: outer awareness of physical, vital and mental sheaths; inner mind in touch with universal mind; the innermost Psychic being or Atman, a spark of the Divine.
la: Explain any one kosha in detail.

Annamaya Kosha, the food sheath, is the physical body formed from the essence of food; it exists by food and goes back to food. With proper exercise and diet it develops; signs are fitness, agility, stamina, endurance, motor skills and eye–hand coordination, and it is the instrument of worship.
Describe the ways for development of the five koshas.

Annamaya: right food, exercise, asanas; Pranamaya: pranayama; Manomaya: good literature, prayer; Vijnanamaya: debates, problem solving, small research, interviewing eminent people; Anandamaya: identifying with fellow beings and the universe.
Explain the theory of trigunas and the right proportion for personality development.

Sattwa (light), Rajas (dynamism), Tamas (inertia) combine in everyone. Sattwik people are calm, Rajasik restless and active, Tamasik idle. Development moves from Tamas to Rajas to Sattwa and beyond; Rajas is needed somewhat, Tamas minimal.
Describe the Panch Koshas and Sri Aurobindo's levels of consciousness.

Five sheaths: annamaya, pranamaya, manomaya, vijnanamaya, anandamaya, with Atman distinct. Sri Aurobindo's concentric rings lead to the Psychic being, and the vertical system rises from the inconscient to Sat-Chit-Ananda.
